title: Find The Duplicate Number
statement: An array holds n + 1 integers, each between 1 and n. Exactly one value appears more than once. Find it. You may not change the array, and you may use only a constant amount of extra memory, so no set and no sorting.

example.caption: The value 2 sits at two indexes. Two different indexes both point at index 2.

idea.sentence: Read each index as a pointer to nums[i]. The duplicate is a node with two arrows into it, so it is where the chain starts to loop, and Floyd's two walkers find that spot.

jargon.plain: Two walkers on one chain: a slow one (one step) and a fast one (two steps). If the chain loops, they must meet inside the loop.
The first node of the loop, the one you reach from outside the loop.

watch.inputHint: One argument: the array, n + 1 numbers each from 1 to n, e.g. [1,3,4,2,2]

vars.meaning: the largest allowed value (the array has n + 1 numbers)

compare.bruteLabel: Remember every number in a set

rows.name: Sort, then compare neighbours
rows.note: Breaks the rule: it changes the array. A sorted copy would cost O(n) space.

rows.name: Hash set
rows.note: Simple and fast, but it stores up to n values.

rows.name: Floyd's two walkers
rows.note: Each walker is a single integer. The array is only read.

fast.takeaway: The set is the obvious answer, and the constraint rules it out. Seeing the array as a linked list gives a loop to detect for free.

stages.title: Start at index 0
stages.note: Think of index i as a node whose single arrow goes to nums[i]. Index 0 is never pointed at, so it is the start of the chain.

stages.title: Race: slow and fast
stages.note: slow moves one step, fast moves two. Because the chain loops, they must meet somewhere inside the loop.

stages.title: Restart slow, walk together
stages.note: Put slow back at 0. Move both one step at a time. The distance maths makes them meet exactly at the loop entrance.

stages.title: Return the entrance
stages.note: The entrance has two arrows into it: one from the tail, one from the loop. Two indexes hold that value, so it is the duplicate.

edges.title: Smallest array
edges.why: Index 0 points to 1, and 1 points to itself. A loop of length one. The walkers meet at once.

edges.title: Same value everywhere
edges.why: The duplicate may appear many times. Many arrows enter index 3, and the walkers still find it.

edges.title: Duplicate is the last index
edges.why: The loop can be tiny and far from the start. The second phase walks the long tail to reach it.

edges.title: Long tail before the loop
edges.why: Most indexes sit in the tail, not in the loop. That is why slow restarts from 0 and walks to the entrance.

gotchas.text: Both walkers start at index 0, so a plain while (slow != fast) would stop at once. Move first, then compare.
Index 0 is the right start because no value is 0, so nothing points back to it and it stays out of the loop. Phase two relies on that.
Use do { } while (slow !== fast) for the first phase. Do not sort the input to look for neighbours: nums.sort() also compares as strings by default and mutates the array.
Go has no do-while. Write for { move; if slow == fast { break } }. Sorting the slice would modify the caller's array too, because slices share memory.

recap.pattern: Linked list: Floyd on an array
recap.key: Treat i -> nums[i] as a pointer chain. A duplicate means two arrows into one node, so the chain loops. Find the loop entrance.
moves: slow = fast = 0. Move slow 1, fast 2 until they meet
Move both 1 step until they meet
